entries.question: What does Vitalos do?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos is a UK-first technology consulting, engineering and digital transformation firm. Its headline is “Modernise. Build. Adopt AI.”, and its supporting line explains it: “We help ambitious organisations modernise operations, build digital products and adopt AI.” One team carries the work from strategy to production and keeps improving it.
entries.fullAnswer: Vitalos works through five practices: Consulting, Engineering, AI & Data, Experience and Managed Services, with Vitalos Labs as a separate research and technical proof capability. You can start with advice, such as an assessment or a discovery, or go straight to engineering when the need is already clear. Whichever route you take, the same standards apply: one accountable Engagement Lead, controlled delivery, quality and security gates before release, and a documented handover. AI sits at the centre of how we advise, build and operate, but we use it only where it creates measurable value. Our brand line, “From strategy to production.”, describes the job: a recommendation only matters if it can be engineered, released and run safely. If you are not sure which service you need, describe the problem rather than the technology and Talk to Vitalos.

entries.question: Who founded Vitalos, and who is accountable for it?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos was founded by Temitope Agbola and is led by its founder. The company you contract with is Vitalos Technologies Limited, company number 16696895. At this stage the founder leads strategy, early client conversations and major risk decisions, and every engagement also has its own named Engagement Lead who is accountable for delivery.
entries.fullAnswer: Vitalos is deliberately founder-led at this stage. Buyers of a young firm should be able to see exactly who is accountable, so the founder is visible and involved: setting strategy, leading the first substantive conversations, shaping engagements and owning major risk and reputation decisions. Accountability for each piece of work sits with one named Engagement Lead, who owns outcomes, scope, risk, quality and reporting for that engagement. The company is also designed so that it does not depend on one person. Standards and decision rules are documented, engagement leadership is assigned, and routine decisions move away from the founder as the team grows. The legal entity is Vitalos Technologies Limited, registered in England with company number 16696895.

entries.question: Why does Vitalos exist?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos exists for the gap between ambition and execution. Many organisations know technology and AI matter, but the hard part is redesigning work, modernising systems, connecting data and carrying change safely into production. The Vitalos mission is to help organisations turn technology and AI into measurable business advantage.
entries.fullAnswer: Choosing a model or buying another tool is rarely the difficult part of change. The difficult part is deciding what should change, making sound engineering decisions and getting new systems live without disrupting the business. Vitalos was set up to cover that whole path. We work with you to understand what needs to change, decide where technology and AI create real value, engineer the products and platforms required, and keep improving them once they are live. That is why Vitalos is neither a strategy-only consultancy nor a build-to-spec agency. The long-term aim is to become the organisation companies call when technology matters, earned through delivered work rather than claimed.

entries.question: What does "From strategy to production" mean for us in practice?
entries.shortAnswer: It means the firm that helps you decide what to do can also build it, release it and run it. You are not handed a report to implement elsewhere. Vitalos ties advice to architecture, delivery and operating reality, and the work can continue after go-live through managed services and improvement.
entries.fullAnswer: The brand line "From strategy to production." shows up in three ways. First, advice has to be implementable: consulting work ends with clear decisions, sequencing, dependencies and success measures, not decorative slides. Second, engineering understands the business context: engineers work from the outcomes agreed in discovery, not from a feature list alone. Third, go-live is not the end: live systems need ownership, monitoring and improvement, which our Managed Services practice provides if you want it. You can still buy one part on its own. Many clients start with a bounded assessment and decide afterwards whether to build with Vitalos, with another supplier or with their own team.

entries.question: What does UK-first mean? Do you work outside the UK?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos launched in the United Kingdom and builds its relationships, references and delivery standards here first. UK-first does not mean UK-only. Contracts, delivery practices and the brand are designed for international work, and Vitalos can serve suitable overseas clients from the UK where legal, tax and data risks are manageable.
entries.fullAnswer: The UK is the Vitalos headquarters, credibility base and primary market, so British English and UK procurement, privacy and accessibility expectations are built into how we work. For clients outside the UK we deliver from the UK first, working with trusted in-market partners where that helps. We do not open offices or entities just to put a city on the website; local presence follows real client demand and local leadership. Before cross-border work we review the contracting entity, governing law, tax, data transfers and any sanctions or local regulatory issues, and we use specialist advice where foreign law applies. If your organisation is outside the UK, Talk to Vitalos and we will tell you plainly whether we can serve you well.

entries.question: Where is Vitalos based, and do you have offices?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos Technologies Limited is registered in England and works UK-first. The firm is remote-capable by design, with in-person workshops and client-site work arranged where they add value. Vitalos does not list offices it does not operate; new locations are added only when there is a real team and real client need.
entries.fullAnswer: Remote working is a normal operating model at Vitalos, not a compromise. Written context, documented decisions and full participation for remote colleagues are standard, and security controls apply wherever people work. When being in the room helps, for example discovery workshops, user research or go-live support, we plan time on site with you. Travel and accommodation are pre-approved and recharged at cost unless the proposal already includes them. Our approach to geography is deliberate: we would rather tell you exactly how we work than imply a footprint we have not built.

entries.question: How is Vitalos different from a large consultancy or systems integrator?
entries.shortAnswer: Large consultancies and systems integrators bring brand, scale and procurement familiarity, but often more layers between you and the people doing the work. Vitalos offers direct senior involvement, one accountable Engagement Lead and engineering ownership in the same team, without enterprise ceremony that does nothing to reduce your risk.
entries.fullAnswer: Vitalos does not pretend to have a global firm's scale, and for some very large programmes a big integrator is the right choice. Vitalos fits well when you want senior people close to the problem, faster decisions and a team that can both advise and build. Our delivery model still keeps the disciplines that matter: a defined lifecycle, mandatory quality and security gates, written scope and change control, and documented handover. What we avoid is process for its own sake, such as long unpaid pitch documents, heavy governance on small pieces of work, or reports disconnected from implementation. Commercially we aim to be sensible: neither the cheapest supplier nor priced for prestige.

entries.question: What kinds of organisations does Vitalos work with?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos mainly works with established UK SMEs and mid-market organisations, typically with around 20 to 1,000 employees, facing operational, technology or digital-product challenges beyond their internal capacity. Vitalos also takes on selected startup, scale-up and enterprise work where the fit is strong, and is building towards public sector readiness.
entries.fullAnswer: Size is a guide rather than a rule. Stronger signals of fit are a clear executive sponsor, a problem worth funding, and processes that still depend on spreadsheets, manual re-keying or disconnected tools, or an ageing platform that limits growth. We also fit well where an internal technology team is capable but needs specialist capacity, or where a previous project has stalled. Poor fit includes buying mainly on the lowest hourly rate, wanting major change without access to decision-makers, users or systems, or expecting us to bypass compliance or overstate results. For public sector and NHS work we are building the assurance and evidence those buyers require before bidding widely.

entries.question: Is Vitalos an AI company?
entries.shortAnswer: AI is at the centre of how Vitalos advises, builds and operates technology, but it is not the whole company. Vitalos is a technology consulting, engineering and digital transformation firm. AI has its own practice, AI & Data, and also runs through Consulting, Engineering, Experience and Managed Services wherever it creates value.
entries.fullAnswer: Vitalos describes itself as AI-centred, not AI-only. That matters to you in two ways. First, we are not selling isolated chatbots or demos: AI is designed into real workflows, data, integrations and operating controls, with evaluation and human oversight where the risk warrants it. Second, we have no incentive to put AI into every problem. If deterministic automation, better integration or a process redesign solves your problem more reliably or at lower cost, we will recommend that instead. The company is built to stay useful whatever the dominant AI technology becomes, because the underlying work of modernising systems, data and operations does not go away.
entries.linkedOfferCta: AI Opportunity Assessment / Talk to Vitalos

entries.question: What is it like to work with Vitalos?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos aims to be organised without being bureaucratic, technically serious without being inaccessible, commercially disciplined without being adversarial, and fast without being reckless. You get one accountable lead, plain reporting on risks and decisions, and honest conversations when scope, timing or budget need to change.
entries.fullAnswer: Our working style follows a few operating principles. Work is tied to an outcome, not just activity. Status reports use evidence and direct language: a project is not reported green simply because people are busy. Risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies stay visible with named owners. Changes go through change control rather than being absorbed silently or argued about later. Documentation is part of delivery, because a system only one engineer understands is not finished. When Vitalos misses something, we own it openly rather than presenting it as a client change. Meetings and reporting scale with the size of the work, so small engagements stay light.

entries.question: What is the Vitalos AI journey?
entries.shortAnswer: The Vitalos AI journey is AI Opportunity Assessment > Prototype > Production > Managed AI. You find and rank the opportunities worth pursuing, prove the strongest with a prototype, engineer it into secure production use, then operate and improve it. Each step ends with a decision, so you invest further only on evidence.
entries.fullAnswer: The journey gives non-specialist buyers a simple way to start, while keeping a route into serious production engineering rather than one-off experiments. The AI Opportunity Assessment identifies high-value, feasible opportunities and readiness gaps. The Prototype tests the business and technical hypothesis quickly against agreed criteria. Production engineers a secure, integrated and observable capability with human oversight where needed, and it can be scaled across further workflows or teams once proven. Managed AI then operates, evaluates, optimises and governs the live capability, because models, data and usage change over time. If earlier evidence already exists you can enter at a later stage, and you can stop at any gate.
entries.linkedOfferCta: AI Opportunity Assessment / Start an AI Opportunity Assessment

entries.question: Can we skip the assessment and go straight to building AI?
entries.shortAnswer: Sometimes. If your use case is already clear, the data is understood and the risks are known, Vitalos can start with a prototype. Where data quality, readiness or risk is uncertain, an AI Opportunity Assessment is the responsible first step, because it tests feasibility and risk before you commit budget to building.
entries.fullAnswer: AI use with uncertain data or readiness is one of the situations where Vitalos requires discovery before build, because building on unknown data creates a high chance of wasted spend or unsafe behaviour. That is a risk rule, not a sales rule. If you have already done the groundwork, for example you have a prioritised use case, representative data and clarity on governance, Vitalos will review that evidence and can move directly to an AI Prototype Sprint. Either way, evaluation criteria are agreed before anything is built, so you know in advance what success looks like and how it will be measured.
entries.linkedOfferCta: AI Opportunity Assessment / Talk to Vitalos

entries.question: Does a successful AI prototype mean it is ready for production?
entries.shortAnswer: No. A prototype proves that an idea can work; it does not prove the system is secure, reliable, integrated, monitored or governed. Vitalos treats production as a separate stage with its own engineering and evaluation, and prototype work does not include production hardening unless that is explicitly agreed.
entries.fullAnswer: Many AI initiatives stall because a convincing demonstration is mistaken for a finished system. Moving to production adds the work that makes AI safe to rely on: integration with your systems and data, security against prompt and data exposure, limits on what tools an agent can use, failure and fallback behaviour, human review where decisions warrant it, monitoring of quality, cost and latency, and change management for model or provider updates. Evaluation criteria must be met before go-live, and production AI passes the same release gates as any other Vitalos system. Separating the stages keeps the prototype affordable and the production system dependable.
entries.linkedOfferCta: AI Prototype Sprint / Talk to Vitalos

entries.question: Which AI models and providers does Vitalos use?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos chooses models and providers per use case rather than tying every client to one vendor. The choice weighs quality on your task, data handling and retention terms, cost, latency, reliability and the risk of depending on a single provider. The model and provider strategy is documented for every production AI system.
entries.fullAnswer: There is no single best model for every job. For each use case Vitalos compares options against evaluation criteria agreed with you, and looks closely at the provider terms that matter to you: where data is processed, how long it is kept and whether it is used for training. Every production AI system Vitalos delivers has a known model and provider, a dependency strategy, versioned prompts and instructions, and a change process for when a model or provider changes. Where it is economically justified, Vitalos designs for portability so that you can switch providers without rebuilding the whole system.

entries.question: Will our data be used to train AI models?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos checks each AI provider's retention and training terms before any of your data is used, keeps confidential data only in tools approved for it, and agrees the training and retention position with you in the contract for any AI system it builds, so you know exactly how your data is treated.
entries.fullAnswer: Training and retention terms differ between providers, and between consumer and business services, so Vitalos checks them rather than assuming. Confidential or restricted client data is never entered into personal, free or unapproved AI accounts. For AI systems delivered to you, the statement of work or AI schedule covers the model and provider, the data and knowledge sources, input and output handling, the provider's training and retention position, and the controls around them. If your policies prohibit certain providers or require particular settings, Vitalos designs within those constraints and records them in the contract.

entries.question: How do you protect sensitive data in AI systems?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos designs AI systems so sensitive data is minimised, access-controlled and kept within approved tools and providers. Systems are tested against prompt and data exposure, agents get only the permissions they need, and prototypes use synthetic data where real data is not essential to the test.
entries.fullAnswer: Data protection starts in design. Vitalos identifies the personal or sensitive data involved, why it is needed, who can access it, where it is processed and how long it is kept, and carries out a data protection impact assessment where the processing is higher risk. During engineering, controls cover access, secrets handling, logging, and security against prompts that try to extract data or misuse tools. Agents are given bounded permissions, and higher-risk actions require human review. Data use for AI is also covered in your contract, including a data processing agreement where Vitalos processes personal data on your behalf.

entries.question: How do you deal with AI hallucinations and wrong answers?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos assumes AI will sometimes be wrong and designs for it. Production AI is grounded in approved sources where relevant, tested against evaluation cases before launch, monitored for errors in use, and given fallback behaviour and human review wherever a wrong answer could cause harm.
entries.fullAnswer: No model is perfectly accurate, so the real question is how errors are detected and contained. Vitalos defines the task and success measures first, builds a set of representative evaluation cases, and checks grounding and retrieval quality where the system answers from your documents or data. Failure and fallback behaviour are designed in, for example passing a case to a person when the request is outside scope. In production, error and hallucination rates, human escalation rates, cost and latency are monitored, and material AI services are re-evaluated as models, prompts and data change.

entries.question: How do you decide whether an AI system is accurate enough to go live?
entries.shortAnswer: Before anything is built, Vitalos agrees with you what good enough means for the task: the evaluation cases, quality thresholds, acceptable error types and when a person must review the output. The system goes live only when it meets those criteria in testing, and the results are kept as release evidence.
entries.fullAnswer: Accuracy is not a single number. A wrong answer in a low-risk drafting task matters less than one that affects a customer, a payment or a person's care, so thresholds depend on the use case and its risk. Vitalos uses representative test cases, including difficult and potentially harmful examples where relevant, and measures evaluation pass rates alongside cost and latency. Where results fall short, the options are to improve the design, narrow the scope, add human review or stop. AI evaluation is one of the mandatory Vitalos quality gates, owned by the AI/Data Lead on the engagement.

entries.question: Will Vitalos guarantee that AI outputs are always correct?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos does not guarantee that AI outputs are always correct, and you should be wary of any supplier that does. AI outputs are probabilistic, so instead of an accuracy warranty, Vitalos contracts set out the evaluation, monitoring and human-oversight controls that keep errors within agreed limits.
entries.fullAnswer: Vitalos contracts describe how an AI system actually behaves rather than treating it as deterministic software. The statement of work or AI schedule covers the intended purpose, known limitations and prohibited uses, evaluation criteria, human oversight and escalation, monitoring and re-evaluation, model change management, and who is responsible for final business decisions. Vitalos also avoids promising a guaranteed return on investment unless a measurable, outcome-based commercial agreement supports it. This is a more honest basis for an AI contract, and it gives your procurement and risk teams something specific to assess.

entries.question: How does Vitalos govern the AI systems it builds?
entries.shortAnswer: Every AI system Vitalos delivers has a named human owner, a defined purpose, agreed evaluation criteria, versioned prompts and models, monitoring of quality, cost and latency, and a change process for model or provider updates. Higher-risk uses add human review, and governance continues after launch through re-evaluation.
entries.fullAnswer: Governance is designed into delivery rather than added as a policy at the end. Before build, the use case, success measures, data sources and risks are agreed. During build, prompts, instructions, models and data sources are versioned, and security and tool permissions are reviewed. Before release, the system passes the AI evaluation gate. After release, monitoring and periodic re-evaluation check that behaviour stays within limits as models and data change, and important workflows have a controlled process for model or provider changes. Auditability is set to match the use case, so you can explain what the system did and why.

entries.question: What are Vitalos's Responsible AI principles?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos applies ten Responsible AI principles: purpose, accountability, transparency, privacy and security, evaluation, human oversight, fairness, reliability, traceability and continuous monitoring. In practice, AI must solve a legitimate problem, a named person stays responsible for it, and it is tested before and after going live.
entries.fullAnswer: Each principle has a practical meaning. Purpose: AI must solve a legitimate business or user problem. Accountability: a human owner remains responsible for each deployed system. Transparency: you understand where AI is used and its material model and provider limitations. Privacy and security: sensitive data is handled deliberately and access is controlled. Evaluation: production AI is tested against defined quality and risk criteria. Human oversight: higher-risk decisions include review or escalation. Fairness: foreseeable discriminatory or harmful outcomes are considered. Reliability: failure, fallback and model change are designed for. Traceability: important instructions, models, data sources and evaluations are versioned. Monitoring: material AI services are re-evaluated as conditions change.

entries.question: Who owns the IP in AI work, including prompts, models and AI-generated outputs?
entries.shortAnswer: Bespoke deliverables you pay for, such as your configuration, integrations and documentation, can be assigned to you, while Vitalos keeps its reusable tools and methods and licenses them to you for use in your system. Raw AI-generated output has uncertain legal status, so Vitalos does not promise exclusive rights in it.
entries.fullAnswer: Vitalos separates three things. Your data, content and background IP remain yours. Bespoke foreground deliverables created and paid for under your statement of work can be assigned to you, subject to agreed carve-outs. Vitalos Background IP, such as evaluation tooling, prompt and tool orchestration frameworks, reusable automations and Labs research, stays with Vitalos, and you receive a perpetual, royalty-free licence to use whatever is embedded in your deliverable. Third-party model and platform terms also apply and are reviewed. Human-authored elements such as architecture, code and documentation can attract normal protection even where AI tools assisted, but the position is fact-specific, which is why the contract states it explicitly.

entries.question: How do you control the running costs of AI?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos treats AI running cost as a design requirement. Model, API and cloud usage is kept separate from professional fees or capped by agreement, cost per task and latency are monitored, and the operating cost of a use case is estimated before you commit to production, so success does not arrive with an unexpected bill.
entries.fullAnswer: A technically successful AI system can still fail commercially if usage charges were never designed into the operating model. Vitalos identifies material variable costs in the proposal, before you commit. During design, options are compared on cost as well as quality, for example by matching the model to the task. In production, cost per task, latency and usage are monitored, and Managed AI includes cost and quality optimisation. Where usage sits inside a fixed fee, it is covered by an explicit allowance or cap rather than left open-ended, and provider price changes are handled through an agreed change process.

entries.question: When would Vitalos advise us not to use AI?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos will advise against AI when there is no clear business or user outcome, when a simpler deterministic workflow or integration would be more reliable, when the data is not ready, or when the risk cannot be governed safely. "Not yet" is a legitimate result of a Vitalos assessment.
entries.fullAnswer: Vitalos is AI-centred, not AI-only, and earns trust by recommending what works. Common reasons to hold back are that the process is broken and needs redesigning first; rules-based automation would give predictable results at lower cost; the data is fragmented or of poor quality; the decision affects people in ways that need human judgement that cannot be properly overseen; or running costs would exceed the value. In those cases Vitalos recommends the alternative, which may be process redesign, integration, data work or simply waiting. You will not be steered towards an AI build because it is the more fashionable answer.
entries.linkedOfferCta: AI Opportunity Assessment / Talk to Vitalos

entries.question: Do you build AI agents, and how much autonomy do they get?
entries.shortAnswer: Yes. Vitalos builds bounded AI agents that carry out defined workflows with controls. Agents get only the tools and permissions their task needs, higher-risk actions need human approval, and sensitive decisions are not handed to autonomous agents without defined oversight. Bounded, measurable workflows come before broad autonomy.
entries.fullAnswer: Agents can save real effort, but an agent with too much authority can also cause real damage. Vitalos starts with tightly scoped workflows where results can be measured and errors caught. Tool and action permissions are written into the design and the contract, agent actions are logged to a level that suits the risk, and failure and fallback behaviour are tested, including what happens when a connected system is unavailable. As evidence builds, scope can widen. Agents are evaluated, monitored and governed like any other production AI system that Vitalos delivers.

entries.question: Will we be locked into one AI vendor?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos works to avoid unnecessary lock-in. It stays pragmatic about vendors, documents each system's model and provider dependencies, and designs for portability where that is economically justified. Managed AI agreements allow controlled model or provider changes for security, availability, cost or quality reasons.
entries.fullAnswer: Some dependence on a model provider is unavoidable, but it should be a deliberate choice with known costs. Vitalos records the provider strategy for every production AI system, keeps your data, prompts and evaluation sets separable from any single provider where practical, and includes change management for model updates so that a provider's change does not silently alter your system's behaviour. Where your long-term flexibility matters more than marginal performance, Vitalos will recommend an architecture that makes switching easier and explain the trade-off openly.

entries.question: Does Vitalos use AI in its own work on our project?
entries.shortAnswer: Yes, where it helps and only with approved tools. Vitalos uses AI to assist research, drafting, design and engineering, but people remain accountable: AI-assisted work is reviewed, AI-generated code goes through normal review, testing and security checks, and your confidential data goes only into tools approved for it.
entries.fullAnswer: Vitalos treats AI tools as governed company systems, not personal conveniences. Confidential or restricted client data is used only in approved enterprise AI workspaces that are consistent with your contract, data processing agreement and the provider's retention and training terms. AI is never the named author or accountable professional on a deliverable, and research claims produced with AI are independently checked. If your organisation restricts AI use on its work or data, tell Vitalos at the start; those expectations are agreed before sensitive work begins and recorded in the statement of work.

entries.question: Can you tell us the return on AI before we start?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos does not promise a return on AI investment before there is evidence. An AI Opportunity Assessment estimates the value of each use case with its assumptions shown, and a prototype then tests that value with your own workflows and data before you decide whether to fund production.
entries.fullAnswer: Value estimates at the start of an AI programme are hypotheses. Vitalos makes them explicit, for example the process cost or time involved, how much of it AI could realistically affect and what would need to be true, so you can test and challenge them. The prototype stage exists to replace assumptions with evidence from your own workflows and data, and production investment is then decided on that evidence. Where an outcome can be measured reliably and enough evidence exists, outcome-linked commercial models can be considered later, but not for early or ambiguous work.
entries.linkedOfferCta: AI Opportunity Assessment / Talk to Vitalos

entries.question: What is it like to build a career at Vitalos?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos offers consequential technology work, close to the problem, where you build what you advise. People get senior responsibility and direct client exposure, consulting and engineering in one environment, AI used as a real delivery capability, and high standards without unnecessary bureaucracy.
entries.fullAnswer: The culture Vitalos is building rewards ownership, candour, craft, commercial sense, clarity, learning, collaboration, respect, pragmatism and client stewardship. It deliberately avoids hero culture, long-hours signalling, blame-driven incident handling, status games between consulting and engineering, and knowledge hoarding. Work is remote-capable by design, with written context and documented decisions, and in-person time is used where it adds value. Technical people can progress without having to become people managers. Vitalos describes only benefits and working practices that are real, and it avoids startup clichés such as rockstars or unlimited hustle.

entries.question: How does the Vitalos hiring process work?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos uses a structured process: screening, a realistic work sample or case exercise, a technical or professional interview, a client communication interview, a values and leadership conversation, and risk-based reference and identity checks. Questions and scoring are structured, so decisions do not depend on who feels most similar to the interviewer.
entries.fullAnswer: The process is kept proportionate to the role. Senior candidates are not asked to produce large unpaid consulting deliverables that Vitalos could reuse commercially; work samples are designed to show reasoning on problems similar to the job. Vitalos hires for judgement under ambiguity, communication, depth in at least one discipline, ownership, respect for engineering and quality controls, commercial awareness and low-ego collaboration. It does not over-rely on brand-name employers, years of experience without evidence of scope, certification counts or puzzle tests unrelated to the actual work.

entries.question: Does Vitalos work with freelancers and associates?
entries.shortAnswer: Yes. Vitalos uses vetted contractors, associates and specialist partners to add capacity and expertise. Associates work under Vitalos security, quality and documentation standards, sign IP, confidentiality and data protection terms, and complete mandatory onboarding. High-performing associates may be offered permanent roles where fit, demand and economics justify it.
entries.fullAnswer: Associates are part of how Vitalos stays lean without compromising quality. Core leadership, client accountability and important knowledge stay inside Vitalos, while associates bring specialist skills or extra capacity for specific engagements. Vitalos assesses employment status properly rather than labelling people by convenience, and access to client systems is least-privilege and removed when an assignment ends. If you would like to be considered for associate work, introduce yourself through the Vitalos contact page with your discipline, experience and availability. Associates are onboarded with the same security and confidentiality requirements as employees.

entries.question: Can engineers progress at Vitalos without managing people?
entries.shortAnswer: Yes. Vitalos has a technical career path to Principal level that does not require becoming a line manager. Its seven-level career framework, from L1 Associate to L7 Partner or Executive, links each level to scope and impact, and titles follow real responsibility rather than tenure.
entries.fullAnswer: Exceptional engineers, AI specialists, designers and consultants can grow their influence through architecture, standards, mentoring and client impact rather than management. People management is a distinct responsibility for those who want it. Promotion needs sustained evidence of next-level scope and quality, appropriate client impact and behaviour consistent with Vitalos principles; it is not automatic after a set time, nor used as a retention tactic. Learning is supported through project stretch, mentoring, design reviews, Labs work and certifications that build real capability.

entries.question: What kinds of partners does Vitalos work with?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos works with partners where there is real value for clients: fractional technology leaders, management and operations consultants, creative and design agencies, managed IT providers, cyber specialists, legal and compliance advisers, and technology vendors. Each relationship has a clear client benefit, ownership model, commercial arrangement and quality expectation.
entries.fullAnswer: Typical partnerships are complementary. Vitalos can deliver the engineering and AI implementation behind a consultant's or fractional leader's transformation work, provide serious platform capability for a design agency, or take on modernisation, product, data and AI projects that sit outside an IT provider's routine support. Specialist cyber, legal and compliance partners give clients assurance that Vitalos does not claim itself. If you see a fit, use the partnership route on the Vitalos contact page and describe the clients you serve and the problems you encounter.

entries.question: Is Vitalos a Microsoft, AWS, Google or Anthropic partner?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos does not currently claim official partner status with any cloud, software or AI provider. Using a technology is not the same as being a partner, so Vitalos describes the technologies it works with accurately and will list partner status only when it meets the provider's actual programme criteria.
entries.fullAnswer: Partner badges can signal capability, but only when they are earned. The Vitalos rule is that a partner claim requires the provider's programme criteria to be met, verified and current. Until then, you will see accurate descriptions of experience rather than logos. Partner credentials may be pursued over time where they help clients, through relevant certifications, joint delivery, marketplace listings or verified programme membership. Any status Vitalos holds will appear in the Trust Centre with its scope. Vitalos will not display a provider's logo simply because it has used that provider's technology.

entries.question: How do we contact Vitalos?
entries.shortAnswer: Use Talk to Vitalos on the website, or email support@vitalos.co.uk. The contact page has routes for project enquiries, specific offers, engineering and AI requirements, managed-service takeovers, procurement and security questions, partnerships, careers and general enquiries, so your message reaches the right person.
entries.fullAnswer: The project enquiry form is deliberately short: your name, organisation, work email, role if you wish, what you are trying to achieve, your timeframe and an optional budget range. You do not need to complete a procurement questionnaire before speaking to Vitalos. The page you enquire from is recorded so that Vitalos understands your context. Personal data from enquiries is handled under the Vitalos privacy notice: it is kept for 24 months after the last contact and is not used for marketing lists. Vitalos is also on LinkedIn.

entries.question: What should we prepare before our first conversation with Vitalos?
entries.shortAnswer: You do not need a specification. It helps to know what is happening today, what it is costing in time, money, risk or customer experience, what has already been tried, who needs to be involved in a decision, what is driving the timing, what success would look like and roughly what level of investment is realistic.
entries.fullAnswer: Vitalos uses the first conversation to understand the problem, not to present a long list of capabilities, so a rough description in your own words is enough. Useful extras, if you have them, include the names of the systems involved, a sense of the data volumes or users affected, and any deadlines set by customers, regulators or contracts. If confidential information is needed before contracting, Vitalos can sign a mutual NDA. By the end of the conversation, you should have a clear view of whether Vitalos can help and what the sensible next step would be.

entries.question: How can our procurement or security team contact Vitalos?
entries.shortAnswer: Use the procurement and security route on the Vitalos contact page for supplier onboarding, security and privacy questionnaires, insurance evidence and requests for controlled documents. Requests are handled by the people who own the evidence, and sensitive material is shared under appropriate confidentiality rather than published.
entries.fullAnswer: The Trust Centre gives you public summaries of security, privacy, Responsible AI, accessibility and resilience, including which certifications Vitalos actually holds. The procurement route is for anything more detailed: completing your questionnaire, providing company and banking details for onboarding, confirming insurance, or sharing policies and contract schedules. Answers reflect what exists today, and Vitalos will tell you plainly where something is planned rather than in place. Company details for onboarding include the legal name, Vitalos Technologies Limited, and company number 16696895.

entries.question: Will Vitalos add us to a mailing list if we enquire?
entries.shortAnswer: No. Sending an enquiry through the Vitalos website does not subscribe you to marketing. Your details are used to reply to your enquiry and discuss working together, kept for 24 months after the last contact and then deleted. Any future newsletter will be a separate, explicit choice.
entries.fullAnswer: The Vitalos privacy notice is clear on this: enquirers are not added to marketing lists, and the website does not use analytics or advertising cookies. When Vitalos contacts business prospects directly, it follows UK direct marketing rules: it identifies itself, gives a working way to opt out, respects objections and keeps suppression records, so that people who opt out are not contacted again. You can ask Vitalos to access, correct or delete your data at any time by emailing support@vitalos.co.uk.

entries.question: How does Vitalos deliver projects?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos uses one delivery lifecycle across the firm: Qualify, Discover, Define, Design, Engineer, Validate, Release, Operate and Improve. Each stage answers a clear question and ends with a decision. The lifecycle is scaled to the work, so a short assessment uses fewer stages than a major platform build.
entries.fullAnswer: The lifecycle exists to make good work repeatable, not to create ceremony. Qualify checks whether Vitalos should take the work on. Discover gathers evidence about the problem. Define turns it into an agreed scope, outcomes and acceptance model. Design covers both the user experience and the technical system. Engineer builds in working increments. Validate tests fitness for use, including security, performance, accessibility and AI evaluation where relevant. Release moves to production safely with rollback planned. Operate and Improve keep the live system healthy and improving. Stages can overlap in iterative delivery, but responsibilities never disappear.

entries.question: When does Vitalos insist on a paid discovery first?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos requires paid discovery when building straight away would create material risk: an unclear problem, complex legacy dependencies, sensitive or regulated data, AI use with uncertain data, several systems to integrate, a major transformation programme, or taking over an unstable system built by someone else.
entries.fullAnswer: Discovery exists to reduce uncertainty, not to manufacture revenue. It maps the business problem, current processes, users, systems, data, constraints, risks, dependencies and success measures before large commitments are made. Where the work is genuinely bounded, discovery is lighter or skipped. Where it is required, it is scoped and priced as its own engagement with defined outputs, so you get value from it even if you decide not to continue with Vitalos. The aim is simple: avoid building the wrong solution at great expense.
entries.linkedOfferCta: Digital Transformation Discovery / Talk to Vitalos

entries.question: How will we know how our project is going?
entries.shortAnswer: You get a weekly status report in plain language, backed by evidence: overall health as green, amber or red with the reason, outcomes achieved, upcoming milestones, decisions needed, top risks with owners, the scope and change position and, where relevant, the commercial position. Larger engagements add regular steering meetings.
entries.fullAnswer: Vitalos does not report a project as green simply because people are busy. Health covers outcomes, scope, timeline, budget, quality, risk, dependencies and decisions. The rhythm scales with the work: active engineering teams check in daily, most engagements have weekly or fortnightly working sessions with you, larger or higher-risk work adds fortnightly or monthly steering, and managed services have monthly service reviews. Risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies are kept in a visible log with owners, and decisions are recorded so you can see why choices were made.

entries.question: How does Vitalos assure quality?
entries.shortAnswer: Production work passes mandatory quality gates before release: architecture, security, privacy and data, functional quality, performance, accessibility, resilience and recovery, operational readiness, documentation and client acceptance, plus AI evaluation where AI is used. Gates scale with risk, but they cannot be silently skipped to protect a date.
entries.fullAnswer: Each gate has an owner and a minimum question. The security gate asks whether material attack, identity, secrets and dependency risks are controlled; the documentation gate asks whether another competent team could understand, operate and change the system. If a gate genuinely does not apply, that is recorded with a reason. If it applies but cannot be completed, the unresolved risk is made explicit, and the accountable release authority must knowingly accept, mitigate or defer the release. Vitalos also uses peer architecture and technical reviews on material work, and senior review for high-risk engagements.

entries.question: How does Vitalos test software?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos testing is risk-based. Depending on the system, it can include unit, contract, integration, end-to-end, accessibility, performance, security, migration and resilience testing, with automated checks running before changes are merged. The aim is useful evidence against real failure modes, not the largest possible number of tests.
entries.fullAnswer: Testing starts with the question of what could go wrong and what it would cost. Critical user and business journeys are always covered. Integrations are tested for failures, retries, duplicate handling and the behaviour of external dependencies. Data migrations are reconciled where the data is financially or operationally important. AI features are evaluated against agreed criteria. Test evidence is kept for release-critical functionality and handed over with the system, so whoever runs it next knows what has been tested and how.

entries.question: Will what you build meet WCAG 2.2 AA accessibility?
entries.shortAnswer: If WCAG 2.2 Level AA is your target, Vitalos designs, builds and tests against it. The accessibility standard is agreed at the start of each engagement and checked before release as a quality gate. Vitalos holds its own website to WCAG 2.2 Level AA and treats accessibility as part of quality, not an after-launch audit.
entries.fullAnswer: Accessibility work covers semantic structure, keyboard operation, visible focus, colour contrast, accessible forms and error messages, alternative text, captions where needed, target sizes, reduced-motion preferences and reflow at high zoom. Designers consider it from the first sketch and engineers test it before release. Vitalos does not display conformance badges without a supporting assessment, and it will tell you plainly where a third-party component or legacy constraint prevents full conformance, so you can decide how to handle it. Accessibility statements are published only after evaluation.

entries.question: How do you make sure what you build performs well?
entries.shortAnswer: Performance is a quality gate. Important routes and workloads are tested against agreed or evidence-based expectations before release, and production systems are monitored so slowdowns are spotted early. Vitalos holds its own website to Google's Core Web Vitals thresholds and can apply the same measures to public sites it builds.
entries.fullAnswer: Performance expectations are agreed with you during design as non-functional requirements, alongside availability, scalability and recoverability. Engineering then builds and tests against them, and performance risk is part of the Technology Health Assessment for existing systems. For public websites, the Core Web Vitals good thresholds at the 75th percentile are Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint within 200 milliseconds and Cumulative Layout Shift under 0.1. Vitalos measures real-user performance where it can, rather than relying on laboratory scores alone.

entries.question: What documentation will we receive?
entries.shortAnswer: Documentation is a deliverable, not an extra. Depending on the work, you receive the statement of work and discovery findings, an architecture overview, architecture decision records, data and integration maps, runbooks, environment and deployment guides, test evidence, a risk log, a decision log and a handover or service transition pack.
entries.fullAnswer: The Vitalos test for documentation is simple: could another competent team understand, operate and change this system without us? Documents are kept concise enough to stay current and useful enough to act on; large static documents that nobody maintains are no better than clear living ones. Code-adjacent documentation, such as decision records, READMEs and runbooks, lives with the code so that it versions with the software. Good documentation also protects you from key-person risk, on your side and on Vitalos's.

entries.question: How do you handle security during delivery?
entries.shortAnswer: Security is designed in, not bolted on at release. Vitalos applies security by design in proportion to exposure, data and criticality, keeps code and infrastructure under version control with peer review, never commits secrets to source control, and runs a security gate covering identity, authorisation, secrets and dependency risk before release.
entries.fullAnswer: Baseline considerations include identity, authorisation, secrets management, encryption, logging, dependency risk, attack surface, supplier risk and secure deployment. Production environments are protected and kept separate from development, production changes are traceable to approved changes, and emergency changes are reviewed and documented afterwards. Open-source dependencies are tracked and monitored. Where your project needs specialist assurance such as penetration testing, Vitalos scopes it separately with a qualified provider. Each client's code, documents, secrets and access groups are kept separate from other clients'.

entries.question: How do you release changes to production safely?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos uses controlled environments, typically development, test, staging and production, with automated checks, peer review and migration control. A release is complete only when deployment, data migration, configuration, monitoring, support ownership and rollback are in place and post-release checks have passed.
entries.fullAnswer: For low-risk engagements, the Engagement Lead and Technical Lead approve releases jointly. Higher-risk or regulated work needs additional security, architecture, client or service-owner approval. A deadline is not approval to skip peer review, validation, backup or rollback planning: if the safe path cannot be completed, the risk is escalated and the decision is made explicitly. Backups are treated as proven only after a restore has been tested, and recovery plans state what can be restored, from where, how quickly and who decides.

entries.question: Do we have to use Vitalos's preferred technology stack?
entries.shortAnswer: No. Vitalos is technology-agnostic and chooses tools to fit your problem, your existing estate and your team's ability to run the result. The tools Vitalos uses to run its own website and operations are not a requirement for clients, and technology choices are recorded with their reasons.
entries.fullAnswer: Technology choices should follow the outcome, not the supplier's habits. Vitalos works across cloud providers, platforms and languages according to client needs, and important decisions are captured in architecture decision records so you can see the trade-offs. Where you have standards, approved suppliers or in-house skills, those shape the design, because a system your team cannot support is a poor result. Vitalos will recommend change where your current technology is a real constraint, and explain why, but it will not push a particular stack for its own convenience.

entries.question: Can Vitalos take over a project another supplier started?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos can take over a project another supplier started, after an assessment. It first examines ownership and access, architecture, code quality, security, data, deployment, documentation and incident history. The outcome can be taking it on as it is, taking it on with a remediation plan, a rescue first, or an honest decision not to proceed.
entries.fullAnswer: Inheriting a system without understanding it is how projects fail twice. The takeover assessment covers who owns the code, infrastructure, accounts, domains, data and licences; how the system is built and deployed; its security posture and known defects; and what documentation and knowledge exist. Vitalos needs administrative access to form a reliable view. Where the system is unstable, the Engineering Rescue offer stabilises it first. Where the risk, access, legality or capability gap makes responsible support impossible, Vitalos says so. It will not accept a service level for a system it has not been allowed to understand.

entries.question: Do you use open-source software in client work?
entries.shortAnswer: Yes, responsibly. Open source is a normal part of modern engineering. Vitalos tracks dependencies, complies with each licence, reviews copyleft and unusual licences before use, preserves required notices, and tells you about material licence constraints, so you never receive rights Vitalos cannot actually give.
entries.fullAnswer: Licence governance matters for ownership. Permissive licences such as MIT, BSD or Apache 2.0 are generally acceptable, subject to their terms. Weak copyleft licences are reviewed for their effect on linking and distribution, and strong or network copyleft licences get legal and architecture review before use in proprietary code. Source-available licences are not assumed to be open source, and code with no licence is not reused. Where it matters, Vitalos provides a dependency inventory or software bill of materials and agrees who handles future dependency updates and security patches.

entries.question: Do you work in an agile way?
entries.shortAnswer: Yes. Vitalos delivers iteratively, in working and tested increments, with regular demonstrations and reprioritisation with you. Agile delivery does not remove architecture, validation, release control or operational readiness, so those disciplines stay in place, scaled to the size and risk of the work.
entries.fullAnswer: Iterative delivery lets you see real software early, change priorities on evidence and avoid big-bang surprises. Vitalos combines it with the controls that keep production safe: recorded architecture decisions, a definition of done that includes testing, security and documentation, release readiness reviews for material releases, and a visible risk log. For time-and-materials work, acceptance can happen sprint by sprint against backlog criteria. Process is kept light on small work and stronger on larger or higher-risk programmes, because the method should improve judgement rather than replace it.

entries.question: Who is accountable if something goes wrong during delivery?
entries.shortAnswer: Your named Vitalos Engagement Lead is accountable for the whole engagement: outcome, delivery health, risk, quality and reporting. Material risks are escalated early rather than hidden, and if Vitalos misses something it owns the problem openly. Technical decisions sit with a named Technical Lead or Solution Architect.
entries.fullAnswer: Vitalos treats escalation as professional risk management rather than failure, so teams raise material risks as soon as the facts point to them, not when a deadline makes recovery impossible. Each risk, assumption, issue and dependency has an owner, impact, response and next action. Decisions on scope, architecture, security, commercial matters and production are made by named owners and recorded. If an issue cannot be resolved at delivery level, it is escalated to senior sponsors on both sides, and the contract provides a formal route if that is ever needed.

entries.question: How do we start working with Vitalos?
entries.shortAnswer: Choose Talk to Vitalos and describe the problem you want to solve. A first conversation establishes context, impact, timing and who needs to be involved. Vitalos then recommends a sensible route, usually a bounded assessment or direct engineering, and sends a written proposal before any work begins.
entries.fullAnswer: The process is designed to be quick for you and honest about fit. After the first conversation, if the opportunity is a good fit, Vitalos shapes an engagement: scope, approach, team, commercial model, assumptions and the logical next phase. You receive a concise proposal covering the problem, outcomes, scope and deliverables, timeline and milestones, team and governance, assumptions and exclusions, fees and payment schedule, and acceptance. Once agreed, the work is contracted under a master services agreement and statement of work, and mobilised with a named Engagement Lead. Material delivery does not start until the agreement is signed or a limited mobilisation has been expressly approved.

entries.question: Will Vitalos produce a free assessment or detailed design to win our work?
entries.shortAnswer: No. Vitalos gives useful perspective during sales conversations, but discovery, architecture and solution design are paid professional work. That keeps proposals honest and protects you too: a design produced for free to win a sale is rarely as rigorous as one produced with proper access and time.
entries.fullAnswer: Vitalos does not give away substantial analysis, architecture, backlogs or assessments as pre-sales work. Instead it offers bounded, paid entry engagements, such as an AI Opportunity Assessment or a Technology Health Assessment, that create useful value even if you decide not to go further. Proposals explain the problem, approach, scope and commercial terms clearly, but they are not long unpaid consulting reports. If you need evidence before committing to a larger programme, the right route is a short paid discovery with defined outputs that you own.

entries.question: How does Vitalos price its work?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos matches the pricing model to the work. Bounded assessments and discoveries are normally fixed-fee. Well-defined builds can be fixed-price or milestone-based. Complex engineering, integration, rescue and research work is usually time and materials with budget controls. Retained capacity and managed services are priced monthly.
entries.fullAnswer: Vitalos does not use one pricing model for everything, because pricing should follow delivery risk and how certain the scope is. Fixed fees suit outputs with clear acceptance criteria. Milestone pricing suits larger programmes that can be split into independently accepted stages. Time and materials suits work where uncertainty remains, and capped time and materials gives you a budget ceiling with prioritised scope. Capacity retainers reserve a defined team each month, and managed services cover a defined operational boundary. For complex work the default route is paid discovery, a re-estimate, then staged implementation. Vitalos will not force uncertain work into a fixed price just because certainty is requested; it creates certainty through discovery, assumptions and staged commitments instead.

entries.question: Do you publish a rate card or prices?
entries.shortAnswer: No. Vitalos does not publish a rate card or fixed prices, because the same offer can describe very different levels of complexity. Proposals set out the scope, outcomes, commercial model, fees and payment schedule for your situation, so you can see exactly what you are paying for and why.
entries.fullAnswer: Price lists tend to push work into packages that do not fit. Vitalos qualifies each opportunity first, then quotes against a defined scope with explicit assumptions, dependencies and exclusions. Fees reflect the responsibility Vitalos takes on, including architecture, quality, security and delivery accountability, not only the hours worked. Pricing aims to be commercially sensible: Vitalos does not compete as the cheapest supplier and does not add prestige mark-ups. Third-party costs such as cloud, AI usage and licences are shown separately, so your total cost is visible before you commit.

entries.question: Can Vitalos give us a fixed price?
entries.shortAnswer: Yes, when the scope is bounded. Assessments, discoveries and clearly defined deliverables are normally fixed-fee, and larger programmes can be split into fixed-price milestones. Where real uncertainty remains, Vitalos proposes discovery first or a capped budget with prioritised scope, rather than hiding risk inside a fixed figure.
entries.fullAnswer: A fixed price needs a defined scope, explicit assumptions, acceptance criteria and contingency appropriate to the uncertainty. If the scope is intentionally vague, a guaranteed fixed price usually ends in disputes or quietly reduced quality, so Vitalos will not offer one in that situation. If you have a hard budget limit but the work is still uncertain, capped time and materials is often the better tool: the cap limits your spend and the scope is prioritised within it. Either way, changes during delivery go through change control, so you always know how the price and the scope relate.

entries.question: What are your payment terms?
entries.shortAnswer: The Vitalos default payment term for private-sector clients is 14 days. Retainers and managed services are normally invoiced monthly in advance, and the invoicing schedule for project work is set out in each proposal. Larger organisations may need 30-day or procurement-standard terms, which Vitalos agrees case by case.
entries.fullAnswer: Billing is designed to match how value is delivered and to avoid large unpaid balances on either side. For project work, the proposal and statement of work set out when invoices fall due, for example on mobilisation, at milestones, monthly or on acceptance, together with whether amounts include or exclude VAT and how pass-through costs are reconciled. Longer payment terms are considered deliberately rather than accepted automatically, because they affect pricing and cash flow. Undisputed invoices should be paid on time; genuine disputes are raised promptly and resolved quickly while undisputed amounts are paid.

entries.question: What contracts does Vitalos use?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos normally contracts through a master services agreement with a statement of work for each engagement. A mutual NDA is used where confidential information is shared before contracting, a data processing agreement where Vitalos processes personal data for you, and security, managed service or AI schedules where the work needs them.
entries.fullAnswer: The master services agreement holds the stable legal terms, so later statements of work can be agreed quickly. Each statement of work sets out the outcome, scope, deliverables, milestones, client responsibilities, assumptions, dependencies, exclusions, team and governance, fees, acceptance, IP treatment, data and security arrangements, and change control. For small, bounded engagements a short-form services agreement can combine the essentials. The Vitalos principle is that the documents must match how the work will actually be delivered, so nothing important, such as ownership, liability, data or termination, is left to implication.

entries.question: Can we use our own contract terms?
entries.shortAnswer: Yes. Many larger organisations prefer their own paper, and Vitalos will work with it. Vitalos reviews it for scope, acceptance, payment, IP, liability, indemnities, data protection, security, service levels, audit rights, subcontracting, insurance, termination and governing law, and raises any changes it needs openly.
entries.fullAnswer: Client terms are not rejected automatically, but they can change the risk and cost of the work. If your terms materially increase liability, insurance, security, reporting, audit or service obligations, Vitalos will adjust scope or price rather than treating the extra burden as free. Vitalos also asks for clarity on which document controls each subject, and avoids incorporating undefined policies that can change over time without a reasonable change mechanism. Purchase orders are treated as administrative unless both parties expressly agree that their terms apply.

entries.question: Will Vitalos sign an NDA?
entries.shortAnswer: Yes. Vitalos signs mutual NDAs where confidential information needs to be shared before contracting, and its master services agreement contains continuing confidentiality terms. Confidential information is used only to evaluate or deliver the work and is shared only with people who need it and are bound appropriately.
entries.fullAnswer: A mutual NDA is usually the better default, because both sides may share sensitive commercial or technical information in early discussions. The Vitalos position covers written, oral, visual and technical information, with the usual exclusions for information that is public, independently developed or already known. Disclosure required by law is permitted, with notice where lawful and practical. Confidentiality is not the same as marketing permission: Vitalos will not use your name, logo or details in case studies without separate, explicit consent.

entries.question: Who owns the code and IP that Vitalos creates for us?
entries.shortAnswer: For genuinely bespoke work created and fully paid for under your statement of work, Vitalos can assign the agreed project-specific IP to you. Vitalos keeps its pre-existing and reusable tools, methods and components, and gives you a perpetual, royalty-free licence to use any that are embedded in your deliverable.
entries.fullAnswer: The Vitalos IP model separates four categories. Your background IP, data and materials remain yours. Bespoke foreground deliverables can be assigned to you once the relevant fees are paid, with an interim licence for testing and use before then where needed. Vitalos Background IP, such as reusable code, frameworks, templates, accelerators and know-how, stays with Vitalos, and you get the rights needed to use, operate, maintain and modify your deliverable. Third-party and open-source components stay under their own licences. Where Vitalos licenses a reusable platform instead of assigning bespoke work, the statement of work says so before pricing and signature.

entries.question: Will we be locked in to Vitalos?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos works to avoid lock-in. For long-lived systems it prefers that production cloud, domain and other strategic accounts belong to you, with Vitalos given named, revocable access. Code, documentation and runbooks are handed over, and Vitalos does not withhold client-owned deliverables after payment.
entries.fullAnswer: Exit is designed in from the start. Statements of work make ownership and licensing explicit, client-owned accounts reduce dependence on Vitalos, and documentation is a required deliverable because a system only one supplier understands is a risk to you. When an engagement or service ends, the exit checklist covers code and repository transfer, documentation and runbooks, credential transfer or revocation, data return or deletion, account ownership, licence continuation and knowledge-transfer sessions. Where a managed service does need Vitalos-owned operational accounts, the contract defines how they are transferred at exit.

entries.question: How do you handle changes to scope?
entries.shortAnswer: Every change goes through open change control. A requested change is handled in one of four ways: swapping it for equal-value scope, using agreed contingency, adding fee or time, or deferring it to a later phase. Small changes are tracked too, because many small changes add up to a large one.
entries.fullAnswer: Scope change is not a failure; unmanaged scope change is. Clarifications within the agreed scope are absorbed and documented. Material new requirements are estimated and handled through a written change order that states the change, the reason, and the impact on scope, timeline, fee and resources, along with any assumptions affected. Delays or dependencies caused on either side are recorded and their impact discussed. If Vitalos misses something it should have delivered, it owns that openly and does not present it as a client change. Material changes to scope, fee or time always need written approval.

entries.question: How does acceptance of deliverables work?
entries.shortAnswer: Acceptance is objective and time-bound. Each deliverable has agreed acceptance criteria, and you normally have 5 to 10 business days to review it. You either accept it or list specific material non-conformities against the criteria, which Vitalos fixes and resubmits. Minor defects are handled separately from acceptance.
entries.fullAnswer: Clear acceptance protects both sides. The criteria are agreed in the statement of work before work starts, so acceptance is about material conformity, not personal preference or perfection. For iterative or time-and-materials work, acceptance can happen incrementally through sprint reviews and backlog criteria rather than in one final event. For suitable business-to-business projects, the contract may include deemed acceptance if a deliverable is used in production or the review window passes without a response, subject to fair negotiation and legal review.

entries.question: Who will work on our engagement?
entries.shortAnswer: Every engagement has a named Engagement Lead, and the team is shaped around your problem. An assessment typically pairs the Engagement Lead with a consultant or architect and specialists as needed. A product build adds product, technical and engineering roles plus quality assurance. AI work adds AI, data and security specialists.
entries.fullAnswer: Vitalos staffs around outcomes rather than fixed departments. Typical shapes include an AI implementation team with an AI/Data Lead, AI and software engineers, and data and security support; a modernisation team with a solution architect, technical lead, engineers, platform specialists and quality assurance; and a managed service with a service delivery manager, reliability and support engineers and engineering capacity. Vitalos does not sell named capacity it cannot credibly provide, avoids single points of failure on critical systems, and brings in specialists where the risk calls for genuine expertise.

entries.question: Do you work remotely or on site?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos works both remotely and on site. It is remote-capable by design and works on site when that adds value, for example for discovery workshops, user research, key decisions or go-live support. The balance is agreed with you at the start, and travel is recharged at cost unless the proposal already includes it.
entries.fullAnswer: Remote delivery keeps costs sensible and lets the right specialists contribute without relocating. It works because Vitalos writes things down: decisions, risks, status and architecture are documented, and remote participants are treated as full members of the team. Time on site is used deliberately rather than as presenteeism. Security controls apply wherever Vitalos people work. If your environment requires on-site access, specific devices or particular network arrangements, tell Vitalos at the start so they can be planned into the statement of work.

entries.question: Does Vitalos use subcontractors or associates?
entries.shortAnswer: Yes. Vitalos uses vetted contractors, associates and specialist partners to add capacity or expertise. They work under Vitalos security, quality and documentation standards and leadership, and Vitalos remains accountable to you. Vitalos does not use hidden subcontracting: you are told when partners are involved and how responsibility is shared.
entries.fullAnswer: Using flexible specialists lets Vitalos bring in the right expertise without carrying permanent cost ahead of demand. The rules are strict. Your contract is with Vitalos, which keeps technical and engagement leadership. Contractors follow Vitalos standards, get least-privilege access that is removed promptly when no longer needed, and sign IP, confidentiality and data protection terms so that rights pass cleanly to you. Critical knowledge is never left with one contractor. Where a partner firm provides specialist capability, the responsibility model is explained to you before the work starts.

entries.question: Can we end an engagement early?
entries.shortAnswer: Yes. Your contract sets out how either party can end the work, including for material breach with a chance to remedy it and, where agreed, for convenience with notice. If you end early for convenience, you pay for work done and any commitments that cannot be cancelled, and an orderly handover follows.
entries.fullAnswer: Termination terms are agreed upfront so that ending a relationship does not turn into a dispute. Typical provisions cover material breach with a cure period, non-payment, insolvency, situations where continuing would be unlawful or unsafe, and convenience termination with notice where negotiated. For fixed-fee or reserved-capacity work, the contract also deals fairly with capacity that was reserved for you. Whatever the reason for ending, the exit process covers the handover of code, documentation, credentials and data, so you are not left without what you have paid for.

entries.question: What happens at the end of an engagement?
entries.shortAnswer: An engagement closes only when acceptance is recorded, outstanding defects and risks are documented with owners, documentation and credentials are handed over, operational ownership is confirmed, and access is removed or transferred. You also get a next-step recommendation, without pressure to buy more.
entries.fullAnswer: Closure is a deliberate step, not just the final invoice or the last merged change. The handover pack gives your team, or a new supplier, what it needs to run and change the system: architecture records, runbooks, deployment guides, test evidence and known risks. If Vitalos is going to keep running the system, project closure and the start of a managed service are separate gates, so project assumptions do not leak into undefined support obligations. Lessons learned are captured, and Vitalos asks, separately, whether you would be willing to act as a reference.

entries.question: Can Vitalos work alongside our in-house team?
entries.shortAnswer: Yes. Vitalos often complements internal teams rather than replacing them. That can mean retained engineering capacity working with your own technology or product team, specialist skills your team lacks, or leading a programme while transferring knowledge so that your people can own the result afterwards.
entries.fullAnswer: Internal teams sometimes worry that a consultancy will create dependency or take over. The Vitalos position is to augment, modernise and transfer knowledge. In practice that means working in your tools where that helps collaboration, following agreed engineering standards, documenting decisions and pairing where knowledge transfer matters. The Vitalos Engagement Lead and your technical lead agree decision rights at the start, so it is clear who decides what. Vitalos keeps its own commercial and people data in its own systems, but day-to-day delivery can happen in your Jira, Azure DevOps or similar tools.

entries.question: Do you offer discounts?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos does not discount simply to close a deal. If the budget is tight, it first looks at reducing or phasing scope, changing the pace or team shape, or a longer commitment or prepayment. This keeps the work properly funded, which protects your outcome as much as Vitalos's margin.
entries.fullAnswer: Discounts that leave a project underfunded tend to reappear later as rushed work or disputes. The Vitalos approach is to trade rather than give: scope, phasing, commitment, payment timing, case-study rights where appropriate, or more of your own team's capability can all legitimately change the price. A straight price reduction is the last option. This applies late in procurement too: Vitalos will discuss the commercial shape with you, but it will not let a late percentage cut quietly turn a healthy project into an underfunded one.

entries.question: What does Vitalos need from us to make an engagement succeed?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos needs a sponsor with authority, a business owner who can make decisions and accept outcomes, access to the people, systems and data in scope, and timely decisions and feedback. These responsibilities are written into the statement of work so both sides know what is expected from the start.
entries.fullAnswer: Client responsibilities are part of the plan, not an afterthought. Vitalos asks for a named client sponsor who owns the business outcome and resolves escalations, a day-to-day owner who provisions access and coordinates people and data, and subject matter experts for workshops and testing. The statement of work also records who is responsible for data, access, security and approvals, and explains how delays in client dependencies affect dates and fees. Vitalos will tell you early if a missing dependency is putting the outcome at risk, rather than waiting until a deadline is missed.

entries.question: Vitalos is new. Why should we trust you with something important?
entries.shortAnswer: Because Vitalos makes trust checkable rather than asking for it. You get a named accountable lead, a written scope with explicit assumptions, mandatory quality and security gates, honest status reporting, and a bounded paid first step that lets you judge the work before committing more. Vitalos never claims scale, clients or certifications it does not have.
entries.fullAnswer: A young firm should be judged on evidence, so Vitalos gives you ways to check. Start with a fixed-fee assessment and see the quality of thinking for yourself. Read the Trust Centre, which lists only controls and certifications that exist, with review dates. Look at Labs and Insights to see how Vitalos reasons about real problems. Read the contract terms: clear IP ownership, client-owned accounts where practical, documented handover and no lock-in. Ask the hard questions in this FAQ and expect straight answers, including where something is planned rather than in place. Vitalos would rather decline poor-fit work than risk a failure it cannot stand behind.

entries.question: What happens if the founder is unavailable?
entries.shortAnswer: Vitalos plans for it. Decisions, risks, architecture and runbooks are documented as the work proceeds, critical responsibilities are paired or deputised, client production environments are never run from personal accounts, and Vitalos avoids single points of failure on critical client systems.
entries.fullAnswer: Key-person risk is real in any young firm, and Vitalos treats founder dependency as an explicit risk to reduce rather than something to hide.
